{{Short description|Data type in type theory}}

In the field of [[type theory]] in [[computer science]], a '''quotient type''' is a [[data type]] that respects a user-defined [[Equality (mathematics)|equality]] relation. A quotient type defines an [[equivalence relation]] <math>\equiv</math> on elements of the type &mdash; for example, we might say that two values of the type <code>Point</code> are equivalent if they have the same respective x- and y-coordinates; formally <code>p1 == p2</code> if <code>p1.x == p2.x && p1.y == p2.y</code>. In type theories that allow quotient types, an additional requirement is made that all operations must respect the equivalence between elements. For example, if <code>f</code> is a function on values of type <code>Point</code>, it must be the case that for two <code>Point</code>s <code>p1</code> and <code>p2</code>, if <code>p1 == p2</code> then <code>f(p1) == f(p2)</code>.

Quotient types are part of a general class of types known as [[algebraic data type]]s. In the early 1980s, quotient types were defined and implemented as part of the [[Nuprl]] [[proof assistant]], in work led by [[Robert L. Constable]] and others.<ref name=Nuprl1986>{{Cite book |last=Constable |first=Robert L. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Z4OzAAAAIAAJ |title=Implementing Mathematics with the Nuprl Proof Development System |date=1986 |publisher=Prentice-Hall |isbn=978-0-13-451832-9 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Constable |first=R. L. |date=1984 |editor-last=Clarke |editor-first=Edmund |editor2-last=Kozen |editor2-first=Dexter |chapter=Mathematics as programming |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-12896-4_359 |title=Logics of Programs |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=164 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=116–128 |doi=10.1007/3-540-12896-4_359 |isbn=978-3-540-38775-6|hdl=1813/6405 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Quotient types have been studied in the context of [[Martin-Löf type theory]],<ref name=NuoLiThesis2015>{{Cite web |last=Li |first=Nuo |date=2015-07-15 |title=Quotient types in type theory |url=https://eprints.nottingham.ac.uk/28941/ |access-date=2023-09-13 |website=eprints.nottingham.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref> [[dependent type theory]],<ref name=Hofmann1995>{{Cite book |last=Hofmann |first=Martin |date=1995 |chapter=A simple model for quotient types |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/BFb0014055 |title=Typed Lambda Calculi and Applications |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=902 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=216–234 |doi=10.1007/BFb0014055 |isbn=978-3-540-49178-1}}</ref> [[higher-order logic]],<ref name=Homeier2005>{{Cite book |last=Homeier |first=Peter V. |date=2005 |editor-last=Hurd |editor-first=Joe |editor2-last=Melham |editor2-first=Tom |chapter=A Design Structure for Higher Order Quotients |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/11541868_9 |title=Theorem Proving in Higher Order Logics |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=3603 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=130–146 |doi=10.1007/11541868_9 |isbn=978-3-540-31820-0}}</ref> and [[homotopy type theory]].<ref name=HoTTBook>{{Cite web |date=2013-03-12 |title=The HoTT Book |url=https://homotopytypetheory.org/book/ |access-date=2023-09-13 |website=Homotopy Type Theory |language=en}}</ref>

== Definition ==

To define a quotient type, one typically provides a [[data type]] together with an [[equivalence relation]] on that type, for example, <code>Point // ==</code>, where <code>==</code> is a user-defined equality relation. The elements of the quotient type are [[equivalence class]]es of elements of the original type.<ref name=NuoLiThesis2015/>

Quotient types can be used to define [[modular arithmetic]]. For example, if <code>Integer</code> is a data type of integers, <math>\equiv_2</math> can be defined by saying that <math>x \equiv_2 y</math> if the difference <math>x - y</math> is even. We then form the type of integers modulo 2:<ref name=Nuprl1986/>
:<code>Integer //</code> <math>\equiv_2</math>

The operations on integers, <code>+</code>, <code>-</code> can be proven to be well-defined on the new quotient type.

== Variations ==

In type theories that lack quotient types, [[setoid]]s (sets explicitly equipped with an equivalence relation) are often used instead of quotient types. However, unlike with setoids, many type theories may require a [[formal proof]] that any functions defined on quotient types are [[equivalence relation#well-definedness under an equivalence relation|well-defined]].<ref name=HofmannThesis1997>{{cite book |last=Hofmann |first=Martin |date=1997 |title=Extensional Constructs in Intensional Type Theory |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4471-0963-1  |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4471-0963-1|isbn=978-1-4471-1243-3 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Properties ==

Quotient types are part of a general class of types known as [[algebraic data type]]s. Just as [[product type]]s and [[sum type]]s are analogous to the cartesian product and disjoint union of abstract algebraic structures, quotient types reflect the concept of set-theoretic [[quotient set|quotient]]s, sets whose elements are partitioned into [[equivalence class]]es by a given equivalence relation on the set. Algebraic structures whose [[underlying set]] is a quotient are also termed quotients. Examples of such quotient structures include quotient [[quotient set|sets]], [[quotient group|groups]], [[quotient ring|rings]], [[quotient category|categories]] and, in topology, [[quotient space (topology)|quotient space]]s.<ref name=NuoLiThesis2015/>
